title: GoodFellas: a personal appreciation of Scorsese's cinematic triumph

commenti.body:
Excellent critique. Something about Goodfellas is just so captivating. It's among Scorsese's most rewatchable films.

And I agree about the glamorizing aspects. Anything that looks glamorous is because the story is portrayed through Henry's eyes from the vantage point of witness protection. He's looking back and absolutely glamorizing his life in the mob.

But anyone who says Goodfellas glamorizes the mob hasn't watched the movie, particularly the "May 11th, 1980" climactic sequence.

I largely agree with your analysis, but just to play devil's advocate for a moment I would say that Scorsese's most accomplished film is actually Silence (2016) which veers away from the highly dynamic style of the films you mention. It was also edited by Thelma Shoonmaker, which shows she isn't always so flashy. 

It follows another line in the director's work that I call "Slow Marty" and includes Kundun (1997), The Age of Innocence (1993) - tentatively, as I haven't seen it and scheduled for me to watch soon - and even arguably Taxi Driver (1976), Raging Bull (1980) and The Irishman (2019). 

I know you include The Irishman in your list of films that are similar to Goodfellas, but I would differ with you on that one. There is actually very little action, the dialogue is sparse and the rhythm of editing is very much in the contemplative style dubbed "transcendental" by Paul Schrader. 

Two that you didn't mention that follow the "Fast Marty" dynamic fast-cutting and flashier style are After Hours (1985) - the earliest in this ramped-up mode - and Bringing Out the Dead (1999) which I really love but gets passed over in discussions on Scorsese.

For anyone interested, my full [Letterboxd review of Silence](https://letterboxd.com/hootsmaguire/film/silence/) argues for its place as the best in the M.S. canon. 

But maybe that's just me being a Wise Guy.

Thanks for your thoughtful response!

I went to see **Silence** in theaters when it came out and I thought it was indeed a great film in a whole different way. A change of pace for Scorsese and Schoonmaker absolutely in terms of style, while the themes of spirituality, Christian guilt and obsession have always been there, going back even to Mean Streets. I'm planning to watch **Kundun** soon as it's probably my biggest Scorsese blindspot. 

You make a very good point about "Slow Marty" and "Fast Marty". I have thought about this myself and I actually found that Scorsese combined those both sides of his personality perfectly in **Killers of the Flower Moon**, which is structured almost like his classic gangster pictures, but at the same time develops at much more leisurely pace and leaves room for more introspection.

I would say that **The Irishman** is almost like the "grown-up version" of Goodfellas. It is structured again like a rise-and-fall story, is firmly set in the gangster milieu and reunites all of his fetish actors from his classic gangster pictures. While much of the action/violence may happen off screen, it is definitely there. But there is indeed a slower pace and more obvious contemplation. I plan to rewatch though, because I haven't seen it since it came out! 

I love **Bringing out the Dead** too! It is indeed overlooked, but it develops like a perfect fever dream and does a great job employing Nicolas Cage's manic energy.

Overall, I think it's definitely debatable which is Scorsese's best film, simply because he has made many legit masterpieces in many different styles, covering many different topics. It's a credit to his versatility that he's also made movies like Silence and Kundun, but when I think of Martin Scorsese, the first thing I about are those rise-and-fall gangster pictures and of those I feel like **GoodFellas** is most exemplary of his style and most enjoyabel/rewatchable.

I re-read your review on Letterboxd and plan to check all your other reviews soon. 

Your comment on ***The Irishman*** is very apt, not that ***Goodfellas*** is any way childish, but that the contemplative style is much more mature. 

Great writing on Scorsese so far, I'm enjoying it very much. I'm planning on watching  ***The Age of Innocence*** shortly, maybe even today, to round out the picture a little.
Thanks for the kind words, let's definitely keep in touch over on Letterboxd!

Looking back at it now, I kind of find Goodfellas overrated in hindsight. It’s very much is a procedural that does a lot of telling, rather showing. The characters also feel rather detached and impersonal

You are of course entitled to your opinion, but I would strongly disagree with your statement that Goodfellas tells rather than showing. There is obviously the voice-over, but there are also so many virtuoso stylistic moments, like the long Copa tracking shot, the perfectly edited (and scored) montages (the editing overall is masterful in this film). It's arguably even those many "showy" elements that have caused people to criticize Goodfellas for its glorification of the mob.

While the glamorousness is telled by Henry,the whole movie is not first-person telled by Henry and Karen,there are far more scenes that Henry and Karen cannot witness with their own eyes.

It is amazing to rewatch the film after being told the unreliable narrortor of Henry,his behavoir all seems suspectful while whole movie didn't change.

I feel something that is so often missed about "Goodfellas" is the way in which Henry is, by gangster standards, something of a softie. He, himself, has really only one foot in that mob life insofar as she doesn't break heads and kill people (much of the time, he's actually trying to be the peacekeeper, like when he tries to intervene for Spider or for Maury).   This quality -- similar to Sam Rothstein in "Casino" --  suits Henry to narrate "Goodfellas" because it makes him more relatable as a narrator. (those who called "The Irishman" a retreading of "Goodfellas" and "Casino" didn't consider the extent to which Frank is a violent man \*a la\* Jimmy Conway; out of the mob trilogy of "Goodfellas," "Casino," "The Irishman," this last is the only one where the main narrator is an actual killer)

Getting back to Henry:  he talks big, almost with a braggadocio about him, and he creates a theatrical impression of the ultimate tough guy by pulling a gun and pistol-whipping the preppie who was harassing Karen.  But there is so much about his character, almost in spite of himself, that evidences  him being cut from a different cloth. For example:

\--His so-called wasting of the aprons on the wounded neighborhood guy. Tutti, of course, remarks, "I gotta toughen this kid up."

\--His making it clear through his actions that he is not the blustering gangster, in his demeanor, that Tommy is;  Tommy's off-hand comment of "you're supposed to be doing this stuff too, you know?" is not insignificant to me.  Tommy, himself, intimidates him with his "funny, how?" speech.  He's more easily intimidated than is becoming for the gangster life.  Henry is well-liked but, if it weren't the case, the likes of Jimmy or Tommy could cause him major problems.  Of course, Tommy says, "I wonder about you sometimes, Henry -- you may fold under questioning."  Which is what ultimately happens.

\--In the second half of the film, Henry is increasingly surrounded by women and children.  His wife.  His little girls.  His girlfriend.  His babysitter. Though not a child, per se, his younger brother.   From the point of view of a goodfella, a gangster, this, too, is evidence of a certain softness.  His "crew" consists also of Karen and of the young babysitter; and they use an infant to smuggle in some of the drugs.  His mother-in-law's house is even enlisted.  His girlfriend's house. By the way needles she him,  Karen is clearly a woman who is not \*afraid\* of her husband; whereas, when faced with the likes of a Jimmy Conway or Tommy DeVito, she likely would be.   This, too, makes Henry more like "one of us."  More like a "normal guy" and not a violent gangster.   

The climactic emblem of this, to me, is when Henry loses a verbal confrontation with the babysitter over a hat.  He backs down; capitulates.   She wins.   An argument like that with Tommy or Jimmy would have gone very differently.   "What could I do?  If she insisted I had to get her hat."  Contrast Henry with a brute like Stanley Kowalski -of "Streetcar" - "I'm the king around here" -- or like a maniac such as Tommy.

Relative to the worldview of those goodfellas, those gangsters,  that softness, tenderness, is a sign of weakness.  It's a negative.  For us -- or for Scorsese, who ultimately is a Christian -- there's something wholesome, relatable, redeemable, about Henry's character, however otherwise amoral he is; casually amoral. 

But when Maury gets whacked, it is Henry who feels bad.  When Billy Batts is killed, it  is Henry who doesn't directly participate and who looks sick to his stomach during the late-night meal. Tommy mother comments on his being so quiet, to which Tommy warns him, really, by saying:  "what's the matter, something wrong with you?"  

He makes for a fascinating character study, which is something that I love about Scorsese feels, generally. The characterization. 

I've just never before heard viewers comment on how much more of a lamb Henry is than the gangsters he surrounds himself with,  so wanted to at least point out that it's a significant part of my appreciation of the story "Goodfellas" tells, especially in contemplation of that dichotomy between "kind-heartedness" (the Christian viewpoint, which is ultimately that of Scorsese and "weakness" (the gangster ethos, as in Tutty's "I gotta toughen that kid up").
